summary: Registers media types for the Ogg container format and sets conformance requirements for implementations of them. It covers the general Ogg type along with variants for audio and video. It replaces RFC 3534, and has been updated by a later document.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 5334 registers three media types for the Ogg container format, the box that holds compressed audio and video. Until then everything was labelled application/ogg, which said nothing about whether the file held music or a film.

The new types split the difference. audio/ogg and video/ogg cover the everyday cases, and application/ogg is kept for complex material such as several interleaved streams with control information. The document also says how to name the codecs inside a file, so a server can tell a player what it is about to send.

subtitle: How the web and other transports should label content that sits in an Ogg container.

tldr.problem: Ogg containers had been exchanged for years under the single label application/ogg. That label hid whether the content was video or audio, and it left parts of the format undefined, so two implementations could disagree about what they were looking at.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5334 redefines application/ogg for complex data and adds video/ogg and audio/ogg for the two common cases, each with its own file extension and Macintosh type code. It also defines the optional codecs parameter and requires or recommends an Ogg Skeleton bitstream so the contents can be identified without decoding.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from September 2008 that obsoletes RFC 3534, and it has since been updated by RFC 7845. The change controller for all three media types is the Xiph.Org Foundation.

today: RFC 5334 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2008. It obsoleted RFC 3534, which had defined application/ogg, and it has since been updated by RFC 7845. The change controller for all three media types is the Xiph.Org Foundation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document describes media types for Ogg, a data encapsulation format defined by the Xiph.Org Foundation for public use. The container format itself is specified in RFC 3533.

Binary data contained in Ogg, such as Vorbis and Theora, has historically been interchanged using the application/ogg media type defined by RFC 3534. This document obsoletes that definition and defines three media types for different kinds of content in Ogg, to reflect this usage in the IANA media type registry, to foster interoperability by defining underspecified aspects, and to provide general security considerations.

The Ogg container format is known to contain Theora or Dirac video, Speex speech in both narrow-band and wide-band forms, Vorbis or FLAC audio, and CMML timed text and metadata. Because Ogg encapsulates binary data, it is possible to include any other type of video, audio, image, text, or, generally speaking, any time-continuously sampled data.

Raw packets from these data sources may be used directly by transport mechanisms that provide their own framing and packet separation, such as UDP datagrams or RTP. Ogg is instead a solution for stream-based storage, such as files, and transport, such as TCP streams or pipes. The media types are needed to identify such content correctly when it is served over HTTP, included in multipart documents, or used in any other place where media types apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Ogg is a box that holds compressed media. The document gives that box a set of labels so that a server can say what is inside it and a player can react correctly.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3534
sections.content: The document lists what changed. The type application/ogg is redefined. The types video/ogg and audio/ogg are defined. New file extensions are defined, and new Macintosh file type codes are defined. The codecs parameter is defined for optional use. The Ogg Skeleton extension becomes a recommended addition for content served under the new types.
sections.plainLanguage: The short list of changes is the whole point of the document: one type is narrowed, two are added, and a way of describing the codecs inside a file is made official.

sections.title: Conformance and Document Conventions
sections.content:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14, and indicate requirement levels for compliant implementations. Requirements apply to all implementations unless otherwise stated.

An implementation is a software module that supports one of the media types defined in the document. Software modules may support multiple media types, but conformance is considered individually for each type.

An implementation that fails to satisfy one or more MUST requirements is considered non-compliant. One that satisfies all MUST requirements but fails one or more SHOULD requirements is said to be conditionally compliant. All other implementations are unconditionally compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets three grades. Failing a MUST makes an implementation non-compliant. Failing a SHOULD makes it conditionally compliant. Meeting everything makes it unconditionally compliant. Each media type is judged on its own, even when one module handles all three.

sections.title: Deployed Media Types and Compatibility
sections.content:
The application/ogg media type had been used in an ad hoc fashion to label and exchange multimedia content in Ogg containers. Using the application top-level type for this kind of content is known to be problematic, in particular since it obfuscates video and audio content. The document therefore defines video/ogg and audio/ogg, which are intended for common use and should be used when dealing with video or audio content respectively. It also obsoletes the RFC 3534 definition of application/ogg and marks it for complex data, such as multitrack visual, audio, textual and other time-continuously sampled data, which is not clearly video or audio and so is not suited to either of the two new types.

An Ogg bitstream generally consists of one or more logical bitstreams, each of which consists of a series of header and data pages packetising time-continuous binary data. The content types of the logical bitstreams may be identified without decoding the header pages through the use of an Ogg Skeleton bitstream. Using Ogg Skeleton is required for content served under the application/ogg type and recommended for video/ogg and audio/ogg, since the Skeleton contains identifiers that describe the different encapsulated data.

It is also recommended that implementations that identify a logical bitstream they cannot decode should ignore it, while continuing to decode the ones they can. Such a precaution ensures backward and forward compatibility with existing and future data.

These media types can optionally use the codecs parameter. Codecs encapsulated in Ogg require a text identifier at the beginning of the first header page, so a machine-readable way to identify the encapsulated codecs is through that header. The document gives a table mapping those header values onto the strings used in the codecs parameter, and keeps an up-to-date version of the table at Xiph.org.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each media type also says what a file must contain. Under application/ogg the file must carry an Ogg Skeleton bitstream, a small map that names the streams inside. Under the two narrower types it is recommended.

The codecs parameter names the encoders inside the file. The identifier for each codec sits at the start of the first header page, and the table in the document maps those bytes onto the names used in the parameter.

sections.title: Relation between the Media Types
sections.content:
The document describes three media types targeted at different data encapsulated in Ogg. Since Ogg is capable of encapsulating any kind of data, the multiple usage scenarios have revealed interoperability issues between implementations when dealing with content served solely under the application/ogg type.

While the earlier definition of application/ogg is redefined, this media type continues to embrace the widest net possible of content, with video/ogg and audio/ogg being smaller subsets of it. The two narrower types take precedence in a subset of the usages, specifically when serving multimedia content that is not complex enough to warrant the use of application/ogg. The audio/ogg type is an even smaller subset within video/ogg, as it is not intended to refer to visual content.

The application/ogg type is the recommended choice for content aimed at scientific and other applications that require various multiplexed signals or streams of continuous data, with or without scriptable control of content. For bitstreams containing visual, timed text, and any other material that requires a visual interface, but that is not complex enough to warrant serving under application/ogg, the video/ogg type is recommended. In situations where the Ogg bitstream predominantly contains audio data, lyrics, metadata or cover art notwithstanding, it is recommended to use the audio/ogg type.
sections.plainLanguage: The three types are nested. application/ogg covers everything, video/ogg covers a smaller part of it, and audio/ogg covers a smaller part again. The rule is to pick the narrowest type that still describes the file honestly.

sections.title: The Media Type Registrations
sections.content:
In accordance with the procedures set forth in RFC 4288, the document registers two new media types and redefines the existing application/ogg. None of the three requires any parameters, and each may optionally carry the codecs parameter whose syntax is defined in RFC 4281. The published specification for all three is RFC 3533.

All three share the same magic number: the first four bytes, 0x4f 0x67 0x67 0x53, correspond to the string OggS. The file extensions differ. application/ogg uses .ogx, because RFC 3534 defined .ogg for it and this document obsoletes that in favour of .ogx, due to concerns where historically some implementations expect .ogg files to be solely Vorbis-encoded audio. video/ogg uses .ogv, and audio/ogg uses .oga, .ogg and .spx. The Macintosh file type codes are OggX, OggV and OggA respectively. All three are marked for common usage, and the change controller for each is the Xiph.Org Foundation.

The restrictions on usage differ. application/ogg should only be used where the data is not suited to video/ogg or audio/ogg; data served under it should use the .ogx extension and must contain an Ogg Skeleton logical bitstream identifying all other contained logical bitstreams. video/ogg should be used for bitstreams containing visual, audio, timed text, or any other material that requires a visual interface, for content not complex enough to warrant application/ogg, for example a combination of Theora video, Vorbis audio, Skeleton metadata and CMML captioning; data served under it should contain an Ogg Skeleton logical bitstream, and implementations interacting with the type should support multiplexed bitstreams. audio/ogg should be used when the bitstream predominantly contains audio data; content served under it should have an Ogg Skeleton logical bitstream when using the default .oga extension, while the .ogg and .spx extensions indicate a specialisation that requires no Skeleton, because of backward compatibility concerns with existing implementations: .ogg is used for files that contain only a Vorbis bitstream and .spx for files that contain only a Speex bitstream.

The document records no interoperability considerations for any of the three types. The Ogg container format is device-, platform- and vendor-neutral, and a broadly portable reference implementation, libogg, is available under the revised 3-clause BSD license. The Xiph.Org Foundation has defined the specification, interoperability and conformance, and conducts regular interoperability testing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each type gets a file extension and a Macintosh type code so that a desktop can recognise the file without reading it. The extensions also carry meaning: .ogg and .spx mean a single Vorbis or Speex stream, while .oga is the general audio extension.

sections.title: Encoding Considerations
sections.content:
The content consists of an unrestricted sequence of octets, so the media type is binary. Ogg encapsulated content is binary data and should be transmitted in a suitable encoding without CR/LF conversion, 7-bit stripping, and the like. Base64 is generally preferred for binary-to-text encoding.

The media types are used for stream-based storage, such as files, and transport, such as TCP streams or pipes. Separate types are used to identify codecs such as in real-time applications for the RTP payload formats of Theora video, Vorbis or Speex audio, as well as for identification of encapsulated data within Ogg through Skeleton.
sections.plainLanguage: The payload is raw binary. If it has to travel as text, it should be encoded, and base64 is the usual choice, because anything that rewrites line endings or strips the seventh bit will corrupt it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Ogg encapsulation format is a container and only a carrier of content, such as audio, video and displayable text data, with a very rigid definition. The format itself is not more vulnerable than any other content framing mechanism.

Ogg does not provide for any generic encryption or signing of itself or its contained bitstreams. It does, however, encapsulate any kind of binary content and so is able to contain encrypted and signed content data. It is also possible to add an external security mechanism that encrypts or signs an Ogg bitstream and thus provides content confidentiality and authenticity.

Because Ogg encapsulates binary data, it is possible to include executable content in an Ogg bitstream. Implementations should not execute such content without prior validation of its origin by the end user.

Issues may arise in applications that use Ogg for streaming or file transfer. Implementations decoding Ogg and its encapsulated bitstreams have to ensure correct handling of manipulated bitstreams, of buffer overflows, and similar issues. It is also possible to author malicious Ogg bitstreams that attempt to call for an excessively large picture size or high sampling-rate audio, and implementations should protect themselves against this kind of attack.

Ogg has an extensible structure, so it is theoretically possible that metadata fields or media formats might be defined in the future which could be used to induce particular actions on the part of the recipient. That capability is currently not supported in the referenced specification. Implementations may fail to implement a specific security model or other means of preventing possibly dangerous operations, and such a failure might be exploited to gain unauthorised access to a system or sensitive information; it is considered out of the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Ogg is only a container, so it adds no new attack surface of its own, but a file inside it can still be dangerous. A decoder has to cope with manipulated files, oversized pictures and buffer overflows, and nothing in the container should be executed without checking where it came from.

viz.caption: What an Ogg decoder has to defend against

items.title: The container is not the risk
items.text: Ogg is a rigid carrier for content and is not more vulnerable than any other framing mechanism.

items.title: No built-in protection
items.text: Ogg provides no generic encryption or signing of itself or of the bitstreams it carries. An external mechanism is needed.

items.title: Executable content
items.text: A bitstream can contain executable content, which should not be run without the end user validating where it came from.

items.title: Malformed input
items.text: Decoders have to handle manipulated bitstreams and buffer overflows correctly.

items.title: Absurd resource requests
items.text: A malicious bitstream can ask for an excessively large picture size or high sampling-rate audio, and implementations should protect themselves against that.
